Europe’s Sauna Economy

Western Europe just found out what happens when you build for fireplaces and get Phoenix. France hit its highest national average temperature ever — not just for June, for any time of year — with 29.8 degrees Celsius across 30 weather stations, while parts of the country pushed over 40. 

More than 60,000–68,000 homes lost power as grids buckled under the extra demand, and at least 40 people drowned in France alone, many of them teenagers escaping to unsupervised rivers and quarries.

By midweek, high‑level heat alerts were up across most of Western Europe: France, Spain, Italy, Germany, Belgium, Britain, Austria, Switzerland and more. 

Spain and Germany were staring down highs around 41 Celsius, with parts of Spain pushing 41–45 in some regions. Britain’s Met Office reported provisional June records near 35–38 degrees, rail companies told passengers to travel only if necessary, and tracks, power lines and schedules folded under infrastructure designed for drizzle, not desert.

The real joke is structural. Europe has spent decades bragging about its “mild climate” and “efficient buildings,” which now translates into homes, schools and offices that trap heat like a sauna and almost never have air‑conditioning.

In Britain, many houses were literally engineered to hold in warmth. In France, AC has become a political Rorschach test — a symbol of inequality, American excess, or climate hypocrisy, depending on who’s complaining.

So you get a continent that can lecture the Global South about emissions, but can’t keep classrooms below 30 degrees or prevent kids from fainting during exams. 

Governments roll out “cool spaces,” drinking fountains and climate shelters — museums as survival pods — because retrofitting millions of buildings is expensive, slow and deeply unpopular with property owners who still think heat waves are a rare glitch.

Scientists are done pretending this is a fluke. Europe is now warming faster than any other continent, last year was hotter than normal almost everywhere, and heat waves are becoming longer, more frequent and deadlier, with tens of thousands of excess deaths in recent summers. 

But the political system treats each wave like a surprise, blames “unusual conditions,” then quietly moves on once the forecast drops back into the 20s — until the next “unprecedented” week arrives right on schedule.

The punchline: everyone tells citizens to “stay hydrated, close the blinds, avoid travel,” because personal responsibility is cheaper than rebuilding the energy grid, redesigning housing stock and admitting that the old climate baseline is dead. 

Europe wants to be a climate leader with stone‑age buildings, Victorian rail, and 21st‑century heat — and it’s discovering that moral superiority doesn’t lower the temperature in a third‑floor walk‑up with sealed windows and no fan.

Here you go frens… who’s going?

The Great American State Fair is a major 16-day national exposition running from today, June 25, through July 10, 2026, on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. (between the U.S. Capitol and the Washington Monument, roughly 4th to 14th Streets).

It’s a large-scale patriotic celebration tied to America’s 250th anniversary (semiquincentennial), styled like a modern World’s Fair. It showcases all 56 U.S. states and territories through pavilions, exhibits, entertainment, and family attractions.

Key Details
Admission: Free and open to the public. Pre-registration is strongly encouraged (walk-ups are welcome). Register here: events.freedom250.org/events/great-american-state-fair.

Hours:
Sunday–Wednesday: 10:00 a.m. – 9:00 p.m.
Thursday–Saturday: 10:00 a.m. – 11:00 p.m.
July 4: 10:00 a.m. – midnight.

Location & Access: National Mall (entry points at 12th & 7th Streets). Strongly recommend public transit (Metro via Smithsonian or L’Enfant Plaza stations) or rideshare—parking is very limited. Security screening applies; no firearms or prohibited items.

What to Expect:
The fair features over 150 exhibits from states, territories, businesses, innovators, and organizations. 

Highlights include:
State and territory pavilions — Each participating state/territory has space to showcase its unique culture, history, products, agriculture, tourism, and traditions (many with hands-on experiences, food samples, or displays).

The iconic 110-foot Freedom 250 Ferris wheel (also called the Great Wheel) — A centerpiece attraction offering panoramic views of the Mall, Capitol, and Washington Monument.21
Family-friendly attractions, carnival-style elements, a restored Smithsonian carousel (in some reports), movie screenings, and live entertainment.

Food vendors with classic fair snacks plus regional American flavors.
Themed districts covering agriculture, innovation/technology, manufacturing, military service, faith & family, education, health & wellness, arts & culture, entrepreneurship, and space exploration.
Military flyovers, musical performances, military bands/ensembles, and daily cultural programming.

The illuminated 110-foot Ferris wheel at dusk on the Mall, with the Washington Monument in the background.

Daily Programming Themes
Thursday, June 25 — The American Canon: Opening Day
Friday, June 26 — Land & Prosperity
Saturday, June 27 — The American Canvas
Sunday, June 28 — Military & Veterans Appreciation Day

🎙 Iran calls for foreign troop withdrawal to ensure regional stability, global energy security

📌 New Delhi, IRNA – Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad has said lasting stability in West Asia and the security of global energy supplies can only be achieved through the withdrawal of foreign forces from the region and the dismantling of US military bases.

Addressing the 11th BRICS Energy Ministers’ Meeting at Gurugram in Haryana, India, on Thursday, Paknejad said Iran remains ready to play an active and constructive role in strengthening energy cooperation among BRICS members to ensure secure and affordable energy supplies.
​
Referring to attacks on Iran’s oil, gas, refining, and petrochemical infrastructure during the recent US-Israeli war of aggression against the country, the minister described the attacks as a blind war against global energy security, saying they had caused damage to facilities, casualties among oil industry workers, environmental consequences, disruptions to supply chains, and economic hardship for thousands of families in the Persian Gulf region.
​
He warned that the consequences of such actions have contributed to energy market instability, rising raw material prices, and increased living costs worldwide, stressing that such attacks constitute a clear violation of international law and the United Nations Charter.
​
Paknejad emphasized that growing energy demand, geopolitical risks, market volatility, climate challenges, and investment constraints require greater international cooperation and pragmatic policymaking. He argued that all energy sources and technologies must contribute to meeting future demand, noting that oil and natural gas are expected to account for more than half of global energy needs through 2050.
​
The minister also proposed the creation of a BRICS energy security partnership aimed at enhancing resilience, stability, and cooperation across the energy value chain among member states.
​
Iran-South Africa Energy Cooperation
​
On the sidelines of the BRICS meeting, Paknejad met with South African Minister of Electricity and Energy Kgosientsho Ramokgopa to discuss expanding bilateral cooperation in the energy sector.
​
The two officials exchanged views on strengthening collaboration and exploring new opportunities for partnership between Tehran and Pretoria in various energy-related fields.
​
Paknejad also held talks with India’s Minister of Housing and Urban Affairs Manohar Lal Khattar during his visit to India.
​
The 11th BRICS Energy Ministers’ Meeting is held on June 25–26. BRICS brings together 11 major emerging economies and developing nations, including Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates.
